question.text:
The compound statement $(\sim(P \wedge Q)) \vee((\sim P) \wedge Q) \Rightarrow((\sim P) \wedge(\sim Q))$ is equivalent to

  1. $((\sim P) \vee Q) \wedge(\sim Q)$
  2. $(\sim Q) \vee P$
  3. $((\sim P) \vee Q) \wedge((\sim Q) \vee P)$
  4. $(\sim P) \vee Q$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Let $\Delta, abla \in\{\wedge, \vee\}$ be such that $(\mathrm{p} ightarrow \mathrm{q}) \Delta(\mathrm{p} abla \mathrm{q})$ is a tautology. Then

  1. $\Delta=\vee, abla=\vee$
  2. $\Delta=\vee, abla=\wedge$
  3. $\Delta=\wedge, abla=\wedge$
  4. $\Delta=\wedge, abla=\vee$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Consider the following statements:
P : I have fever
Q: I will not take medicine
R : I will take rest.
The statement "If I have fever, then I will take medicine and I will take rest" is equivalent to :

  1. $((\sim P) \vee \sim Q) \wedge((\sim P) \vee \sim R)$
  2. $(P \vee \sim Q) \wedge(P \vee \sim R)$
  3. $((\sim P) \vee \sim Q) \wedge((\sim P) \vee R)$
  4. $(P \vee Q) \wedge((\sim P) \vee R)$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
If $p, q$ and $r$ are three propositions, then which of the following combination of truth values of $p, q$ and $r$ makes the logical expression $\{(p \vee q) \wedge((\sim p) \vee r)\} \rightarrow((\sim q) \vee r)$ false?

  1. $p=F, q=T, r=F$
  2. $p=T, q=T, r=F$
  3. $p=T, q=F, r=T$
  4. $p=T, q=F, r=F$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Among the two statements
(S1) : $(p \Rightarrow q) \wedge(p \wedge(\sim q))$ is a contradiction and
(S2) : $(p \wedge q) \vee((\sim p) \wedge q) \vee(p \wedge(\sim q)) \vee((\sim p) \wedge(\sim q))$ is a tautology

  1. both are false.
  2. only (S1) is true.
  3. both are true.
  4. only (S2) is true.
question.subject: Mathematical Logic
